story: The Atlas lists 2 studies with Peter M Finan as a middle author. DIB2012 reports TBC1D7 as the third core subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, the complex that holds back Rheb and mTORC1 (a cell-culture study). DUV2010 reports cells with a permanently active mTORC1 (TSC2 loss), with rapamycin as a control, showing that mTORC1 activation is enough to switch on glycolysis, the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and fat synthesis.

PubMed gives no affiliation for this author in the Atlas papers. The identity was checked through a related paper with several of the same co-authors, which lists Peter M Finan at Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, together with co-authors from both Atlas papers. The Atlas papers combine a Harvard group with Novartis scientists.

studies.title: TBC1D7 is a third subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex upstream of mTORC1
studies.finding: TBC1D7 is the third core subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex regulating Rheb/mTORC1.

studies.title: Activation of a metabolic gene regulatory network downstream of mTOR complex 1
studies.finding:
Used cells with constitutively active mTORC1 (TSC2 loss) and rapamycin to map what mTORC1 switches on besides protein synthesis. Gene expression and metabolite profiling showed that mTORC1 activation is enough to drive glycolysis, the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and de novo lipid synthesis. This ran through a transcriptional program of HIF1alpha and SREBP1/2 target genes; SREBP1 and 2 were needed for proliferation downstream of mTORC1, and their activation required S6K1.
Boundary: cultured cells, mostly mouse fibroblasts with genetic mTORC1 activation; tissue and human relevance not tested here.

current.lab_name: Novartis Oncology (Florham Park, New Jersey, USA)
current.role: Co-author (middle position in the author list) of the Atlas studies MOT2008, BIS2013, BAS2012, YAO2011, FRA2013.
current.sub: Novartis Oncology, Florham Park, NJ, USA
story: MOT2008 (2008) is a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in metastatic kidney cancer in which everolimus extended median progression-free survival from 1.9 to 4.0 months. David Lebwohl is a middle author in the author list. BIS2013 (2013) is a phase 3 randomised trial (118 people) of everolimus for kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex or LAM. Tumours shrank by at least half in 42% of treated people and in none on placebo. David Lebwohl is a middle author in the author list. BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Adding everolimus to exemestane roughly doubled progression-free survival (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review). David Lebwohl is a middle author in the author list. YAO2011 (2011) is RADIANT-3, a phase 3 randomised trial (410 people) in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. Everolimus raised median progression-free survival from 4.6 to 11.0 months. David Lebwohl is a middle author in the author list. FRA2013 (2013) is a phase 3 randomised trial (117 people) of everolimus for brain tumours called SEGA in tuberous sclerosis. Tumours shrank by at least half in 35% of treated people and in none on placebo. David Lebwohl is a middle author in the author list.

No Atlas record gives an affiliation for this author. The affiliation here comes from related Novartis-sponsored everolimus papers, where PubMed or the paper's own author list places the same named author at Novartis in Florham Park, New Jersey.

studies.finding: Everolimus extended median progression-free survival from 1.9 to 4.0 months versus placebo in metastatic renal cell carcinoma.

studies.title: Everolimus for angiomyolipoma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex or sporadic lymphangioleiomyomatosis (EXIST-2): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
studies.finding: The companion phase 3 RCT (n=118) to EXIST-1, targeting kidney tumors (angiomyolipomas) in tuberous sclerosis and LAM. Everolimus shrank them by >=50% in 42% of patients versus 0% on placebo. Together EXIST-1 and -2 sealed everolimus as a disease-modifying therapy across multiple TSC tumor types.

studies.title: Everolimus in postmenopausal hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer (BOLERO-2)
studies.finding: A phase 3 RCT (n=724) proving mTOR matters in a common cancer. Resistance to hormone therapy in breast cancer is associated with mTOR activation. Adding everolimus more than doubled progression-free survival (10.6 vs 4.1 months by central review) - leading to FDA approval. Main toxicity was stomatitis.

studies.title: Everolimus for advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (RADIANT-3)
studies.finding: A phase 3 RCT (n=410) that made everolimus a standard treatment for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. It more than doubled progression-free survival (11.0 vs 4.6 months, a 65% reduction in risk of progression/death) with mostly mild side effects. Another FDA-approved indication built on blocking mTOR.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (EXIST-1): a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
studies.finding: Phase 3 RCT (n=117) in tuberous sclerosis, the disease where mTOR is stuck ON by a genetic fault. Everolimus shrank brain tumors (SEGA) by >=50% in 35% of patients versus 0% on placebo. Because the underlying cause here is direct mTOR overactivation, this is arguably the cleanest randomised human evidence that blocking mTOR works in a genetically defined mTORopathy -- which does not extend to mTOR inhibition in people without such a mutation.

story: Rogerio M Castilho was first author of a 2009 paper in Cell Stem Cell. PubMed lists the author in the Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch of the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the US National Institutes of Health.

In mice, constant Wnt signalling first made hair follicles grow fast, then wore out the skin stem cells and caused hair loss. This depended on mTOR, and rapamycin rescued the effect. The study suggests mTOR can push stem cells into senescence when growth signals never stop. It was done in mice.

story: Penny Lovat is a middle author on two cell-biology papers in the Atlas, both from groups at Newcastle University. PubMed lists her in the Institute of Cellular Medicine in 2017 and in the Translation and Clinical Research Institute in 2024.

The 2017 paper explains why mTORC1 stays active in senescent human cells even when nutrients are removed. The 2024 paper shows that healthy human cells clear damaged mitochondria all the time, that this stops in senescent and aged cells, and that restarting it with a small molecule improved markers of aging in cells. Both studies used cultured cells.

studies.title: Persistent mTORC1 signaling in cell senescence results from defects in amino acid and growth factor sensing
studies.finding: Explains why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells. In human fibroblasts rendered senescent three different ways, mTORC1 is constitutively active and no longer responds to serum or amino acid withdrawal. The defect is upstream, not in mTORC1 itself: it is driven in part by depolarisation of the senescent plasma membrane, which leads to primary cilia defects and a failure to shut off growth-factor signalling, while increased autophagy and high intracellular amino acid levels may act to support the nutrient arm. Correcting these inputs restored sensitivity of the pathway and killed the cells, which frames persistent mTORC1 signalling as a survival dependency of senescent cells rather tha

studies.title: Suppressed basal mitophagy drives cellular aging phenotypes that can be reversed by a p62-targeting small molecule
studies.finding: Healthy primary human cells run a high level of basal mitophagy, started by mitochondrial superoxide and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the selective receptor. That housekeeping shuts down on entry into senescence and in naturally aged cells. Blocking mitophagy in young proliferating cells was by itself enough to trigger the senescence program, and reactivation of mitophagy was necessary for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin and of NAD precursors, which places part of rapamycin's action on cellular ageing downstream of mitochondrial quality control rather than beside it. A p62-targeting small molecule restored mitophagy and rescued markers of cellular ageing.

story: Jiajie Tao was first author of the Atlas study TAO2026, done in a carnivorous fish. In the liver, the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway helps decide whether glucose is turned into fat or stored as glycogen. In this fish the pathway is impaired, and that goes together with a heavy build-up of liver glycogen that resembles glucose intolerance. This is an animal study, and the finding is an association. PubMed lists Tao at Shanghai Ocean University.

current.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, University of Oulu (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Piia Lassila was first author of a 2026 study from the University of Oulu (LASSILA2026). In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin raised the liver-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7 percent. In male mice, activating the receptor PXR enlarged the liver and raised AKT-MTOR activity, but not YAP activity.

highlights.LASSILA2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu.

pubmed_affiliation: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Biocenter Oulu, Medical Research Center Oulu, Oulu University Hospital, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland.

studies.title: Pregnane X receptor-mediated liver growth: a controlled clinical trial in healthy volunteers and identification of the role of AKT-MTOR pathway in mouse.
studies.finding: One week of rifampicin increased the liver volume-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7% in 16 healthy volunteers, and PXR activation enlarged the liver in male mice, accompanied by increased AKT-MTOR pathway activity, without YAP activation.

current.lab_name: Revolution Medicines (Redwood City, California, USA)
current.role: Co-author of two papers on the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors RMC-6272 (2023) and RMC-5552 (2025).
current.sub: Revolution Medicines, Redwood City (PubMed affiliation, 2023–2025)
story: Yu Chi Yang is a middle author on two Atlas papers about bi-steric drugs that block mTORC1 more than mTORC2. The 2023 preclinical paper showed RMC-6272 overcame resistance in breast cancer cells and mouse tumours (MEN2023). The 2025 phase 1 trial of RMC-5552 in 57 people with advanced solid tumours had low rates of high blood sugar and a 64 percent disease control rate (SCH2025). That trial had no comparison group.
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biology at Revolution Medicines on the first paper and at Revolution Medicines on the second.

highlights.MEN2023: Middle author; PubMed lists the affiliation as the Department of Biology at Revolution Medicines.
highlights.SCH2025: Middle author of the phase 1 trial; PubMed lists Revolution Medicines.

pubmed_affiliation: Revolution Medicines, Redwood City, California.

studies.title: A bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor overcomes drug resistance in breast cancer
studies.finding: RMC-6272, a bi-steric molecule with >25-fold selectivity for mTORC1 over mTORC2, completely suppresses mTORC1 (hitting the rapamycin-resistant substrate 4E-BP1) and overcomes hormone- and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance in breast cancer cell lines and PDX -- the preclinical basis for the RMC-5552 selective-inhibitor clinical program.

studies.title: The Bi-steric, mTORC1-Selective Inhibitor, RMC-5552, in Advanced Solid Tumors: A Phase 1 Trial
studies.finding: First-in-human, open-label dose-escalation trial (n=57, advanced solid tumors, no comparator arm) of a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor. Treatment-related hyperglycemia was low (4%) and not dose-limiting, alongside a 64% disease control rate. Because the trial was uncontrolled and made no head-to-head comparison against rapamycin or an ATP-site inhibitor, this is encouraging early clinical evidence consistent with the hypothesis that sparing mTORC2 reduces metabolic toxicity -- it does not establish mTORC2 sparing as the cause.

current.lab_name: Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
current.role: Co-author of two Atlas studies, one on rapamycin and senescent cells and one on growth hormone receptor deletion in mice.
current.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · UT Health San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Yuji Ikeno is a middle author on two Atlas studies. The 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper found that rapamycin lowers the inflammatory signals of senescent cells by cutting the translation of IL1A, and that it reduced the ability of senescent cells to help prostate tumors grow in mice.

The 2026 Aging Cell paper found that deleting the growth hormone receptor in middle-aged mice extended lifespan. PubMed lists him at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies in San Antonio in both papers.

highlights.LAB2015: Middle author of the study showing that mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype through IL1A translation.
highlights.DUR2026: Middle author of the mouse study of growth hormone receptor deletion at 12 months of age.

pubmed_affiliation: Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, San Antonio, Texas, USA.

studies.title: mTOR regulates the pro-tumorigenic senescence-associated secretory phenotype by promoting IL1A translation
studies.finding: Explained HOW rapamycin calms 'inflammaging'. Senescent cells spew inflammatory signals (the SASP) that damage surrounding tissue and even feed tumors. mTOR powers this by translating IL1A, the cytokine at the top of the cascade. Rapamycin selectively shuts it down - and blocked senescent cells from fueling prostate tumor growth in mice.

studies.title: Midlife Growth Hormone Receptor Ablation Extends Healthy Lifespan and Induces Sex-Specific Hepatic Transcriptional Changes at Single-Cell Resolution
studies.finding: Deleting the growth hormone receptor in mice at 12 months of age, in middle age and long after development is complete, still significantly extended lifespan in both sexes without major effects on body growth. Males showed improved insulin sensitivity and were protected against age-related decline in neuromuscular performance and bone microarchitecture despite increased adiposity. Liver snRNA-seq revealed sex-dimorphic remodelling, including a shift toward feminised gene expression in male hepatocytes consistent with loss of pulsatile GH-STAT5 signalling. story: In SCH2025 (2025), Howard A Burris is a co-author in the middle of the author list; the paper is a first-in-human phase 1 trial of RMC-5552, an mTORC1-selective inhibitor, in 57 people with advanced solid tumors. It had no comparison group, so it is early evidence.

In PIC2014 (2014), Howard A Burris is a co-author in the middle of the author list; the paper is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2, a double-blind phase 3 trial of everolimus plus exemestane versus placebo plus exemestane in postmenopausal women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. PubMed lists the affiliation as: Sarah Cannon Research Institute, Nashville, Tennessee. Other Atlas papers under the same name could not be checked against PubMed affiliations, so they are not covered here.

highlights.PIC2014: Co-author of this paper, BOLERO-2 final survival report.

studies.title: Everolimus plus exemestane for hormone-receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor-2-negative advanced breast cancer: overall survival results from BOLERO-2†
studies.finding: This is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2, the phase III double-blind trial (published primary analysis: BAS2012) in which postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had progressed on a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor received exemestane 25 mg/day plus either everolimus 10 mg/day or placebo. The primary endpoint, progression-free survival by local investigator, remained improved: median 7.8 vs 3.2 months (P < 0.0001), a 4.6-month gain. current.lab_name: School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield (Sheffield, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: First author of a 2026 study on collagen I, amino acid uptake and mTORC1 in cancer cells.
current.sub: School of Biosciences · University of Sheffield, United Kingdom
story: The study found that collagen I, a protein that is common around tumours, switches on mTORC1 through an integrin receptor and moves the amino acid transporter LAT1-4F2hc to the cell membrane. This keeps cancer cells supplied with essential amino acids and alive where nutrients are scarce. The transporter was also higher in basal-like breast and pancreatic tumours, where it tracked with poor outcomes. Nazemi is the first of six authors, and PubMed lists the University of Sheffield.

highlights.NAZ2026: First of six authors on the study of collagen I driving amino acid import and mTORC1 activity in cancer cells.

pubmed_affiliation: School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, United Kingdom.

studies.title: Collagen I promotes cancer cell survival via amino acid import and mTORC1/S6 activation
studies.finding: Collagen I drives alpha2beta1 integrin-dependent mTORC1/S6 activation and membrane localization of the LAT1-4F2hc amino acid transporter, sustaining essential amino acid supply and cancer cell survival in nutrient-poor, collagen-rich tumor stroma; LAT1-4F2hc is upregulated in basal-like breast/pancreatic tumors and correlates with poor prognosis.

current.lab_name: School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
current.role: Last author of a mouse study of microplastic and DEHP exposure, mTOR and autism-like behaviour.
current.sub: School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University
story: Rui Li was last author of the Atlas study YANG2026 in Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety. Young mice were given polypropylene microplastics and the plasticizer DEHP. They developed autism-like behaviour, and the brain showed mTOR activation with impaired autophagy. Rapamycin restored autophagic flux and eased the behaviour changes. It is a mouse study. PubMed lists Li at Central China Normal University in Wuhan.

highlights.YANG2026: Last author: senior author of the mouse study linking microplastic and DEHP exposure to mTOR-driven autophagy impairment.

pubmed_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Pesticide & Chemical Biology of the Ministry of Education, Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University, Wuhan 430079, China.

studies.title: Early-life exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP induces ASD-relevant neurodevelopmental alterations involving mTOR-regulated autophagy impairment
studies.finding: PP-MPs and DEHP activate mTOR and impair autophagy, inducing ASD-like neurodevelopmental deficits in mice; rapamycin rescues autophagic flux and social/behavioral phenotypes.

current.lab_name: School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)
current.role: First author of the cryo-EM structure study of the amino-acid transporter SLC36A1 (PAT1).
current.sub: State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University
story: Jian Yin was first author of the Atlas study YIN2026 in Nature Communications. The team solved cryo-EM structures of human PAT1 (SLC36A1) alone and bound to three different substrates. All three sit in a similar spot, which explains why PAT1 accepts so many amino acid-like molecules. This is a structure study. PAT1's links to lysosomal amino acid export and mTORC1 come from earlier work. PubMed lists Yin at Tsinghua University.

highlights.YIN2026: First author: reported the cryo-EM structures of human PAT1 (SLC36A1) with different substrates.

pubmed_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology, Ministry of Education Key Laboratory of Protein Science, Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Structural Biology, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China.

studies.title: Substrate recognition and transport mechanism of the human proton-coupled amino-acid transporter 1 (SLC36A1)
studies.finding: Cryo-EM structures of human PAT1 (SLC36A1) in apo and substrate-bound states reveal a convergent binding mode for diverse zwitterionic amino acids. This is a structural study; PAT1's role in lysosomal amino acid export and mTORC1 activation comes from earlier work.

current.lab_name: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China)
current.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study on Lamtor5 loss, macrophage ageing and systemic ageing.
current.sub: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, China · Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University, China
story: Nianyin Lv was first author of a 2026 mouse study on how the immune system ages. Lamtor5 is a subunit of a lysosomal complex that activates mTOR. The study found that its levels fall with age, and that losing it makes macrophages (immune cells) senescent. Those cells release signals through cGAS-STING that drive inflammation and ageing features in the whole animal. Putting Lamtor5 back in aged mice reduced these signs. PubMed lists Lv at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine and at Zhejiang Shuren University.

highlights.LV2026: First author of the study linking falling Lamtor5 to macrophage senescence and ageing in mice.

pubmed_affiliation: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, Nanjing, China.

studies.title: Age-associated decline of Lamtor5 drives immunosenescence and systemic aging via cGAS-mediated paracrine inflammation.
studies.finding: Age-driven loss of Lamtor5, a key lysosomal mTOR activation complex subunit, drives macrophage immunosenescence and systemic aging phenotypes in mice by unleashing cGAS-STING paracrine inflammation; restoring Lamtor5 in aged mice rescued immunosenescence and attenuated systemic ageing phenotypes.
